finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> enforces no authorization: is_allowed returns a bool that is discarded, so any caller can delete any file.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP DELETE request to /files/<fid>; no header required.

trace.note: is_allowed imported under alias require_allowed; ensure_allowed is a separate aborting function
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') result discarded, no abort

finding.guards_checked: before_request (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user; is_allowed returns bool with no abort; no ownership or authentication check. Fix: use ensure_allowed at line 18.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. before_request (views.py:10-12) only copies a client-supplied header into g.user and enforces nothing. The check at views.py:18 is require_allowed(...), an alias for acl.is_allowed, which returns a bool (acl.py:5) and never aborts. Its result is a bare statement, so it is discarded, and del STORE[fid] runs at views.py:19. The aborting ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) is imported at views.py:3 but not called on the delete route.
verdict.reason: The DELETE route at views.py:15-19 has no effective authorization: the bool returned by is_allowed (acl.py:5) is discarded by the bare call at views.py:18, so views.py:19 deletes the file for any caller, including an anonymous one with no X-Session-User-Verified header.

finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header with no verification, so any caller can impersonate any user for authorization decisions.
finding.sink: g.user used in ensure_allowed (views.py:26) and require_allowed (views.py:18)

trace.note: header copied into g.user with no signature or session check

finding.guards_checked: No verification in this code. The header name suggests an upstream proxy verifies it, but nothing here signs, validates, or strips inbound copies. Impact depends on deployment; critical if the header is not overwritten upstream.

verdict.guard_found: None in the code. views.py:12 copies the header into g.user with no signature, session, or proxy-strip check. acl.py:4-10 is a plain allowlist lookup keyed on that identity. The result of ensure_allowed at views.py:26 is not discarded: acl.py:9-10 aborts with 403 when the check fails, so it is a real gate, but it only tests the spoofable identity. require_allowed (views.py:18) is an alias for is_allowed (views.py:4), which returns a bool. Its result is never tested, so the delete handler at views.py:18-19 has no effective check for any caller.
verdict.reason: The rename path holds: the header is copied unverified at views.py:12, reaches the identity lookup at acl.py:5 through ensure_allowed at views.py:26 and acl.py:9-10, and nothing in this code verifies it, so an attacker who sends a chosen header value can impersonate a granted user. The trace is marked false because the candidate lists views.py:18 as an identity-based sink, but that call discards a bool from is_allowed, so delete is unauthorized for every caller and does not depend on the spoofed identity; this is a separate, more severe defect the candidate misdescribed. Exploitability in production still depends on whether an upstream proxy strips and overwrites inbound copies of this header, which this code cannot show.

finding.claim: Missing file IDs raise an unhandled KeyError (HTTP 500), and the 500 vs 403 difference reveals whether a given file ID exists.
finding.source: <fid> path parameter in DELETE /files/<fid> and POST /files/<fid>/rename.

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for unknown fid

finding.guards_checked: No existence check and no 404 handler.

verdict.guard_found: None blocks the KeyError. views.py:17 and views.py:25 do the STORE[fid] lookup before any ACL check, and there is no existence check or 404 handler in views.py. The before_request hook at views.py:10-12 only sets g.user. The ACL calls at views.py:18 and views.py:26 run after the lookup, so they never get a chance to block it. For the oracle itself, acl.py:4-10 is only reached for existing files. Separately, views.py:18 calls require_allowed (acl.is_allowed, which returns a bool) as a bare statement and discards the result, so DELETE has no effective authorization at all. That is a stronger finding than the one candidate reported.
verdict.reason: The lines at views.py:17 and views.py:25 do what the candidate says, and nothing between the request and that lookup stops a missing ID from raising KeyError (500), while an existing ID reaches the ACL and returns 403 (rename, acl.py:10) or proceeds (delete, views.py:18 discards the bool). Anonymous or low-privilege callers can reach both endpoints, so the 500-vs-non-500 difference reveals whether a file ID exists. Severity is low because it is an existence oracle, not a data read.

finding.claim: Rename handler does not validate the JSON body: a missing or non-JSON body causes a 500, and the name value is stored with no type or length check.

trace.note: request.json may be None or non-dict; name stored unchecked

finding.guards_checked: No type or length validation. No rendering or query sink in the audited files, so no injection claimed; downstream use of name is out of scope.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write") at views.py:26 calls acl.py:8-10, which aborts with 403 unless is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) finds "write" in the file's grants for g.user. Only a caller who already holds write permission reaches views.py:27.
verdict.reason: Line views.py:27 exists and does what the trace says, but the attacker must already hold a "write" grant, which views.py:26 enforces via ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, abort(403)), so the unvalidated name is set only by a user who already has that power and the finding is not a security vulnerability. The 500 claim is also overstated: a missing key or non-dict JSON raises and yields a 500, but a non-JSON body makes Flask's request.json return a 400/415 rather than a 500, and any such failure affects only the caller's own request.
